name: room
text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Do this: Run a weekly automated scan of all prompts in our system, flagging duplicates and near-duplicates, then route the report to the lead for review. This keeps broken prompts out of production by catching them before they merge, not after. The trade-off is speed—we delay merges by a week to catch issues—but we avoid the higher cost of fixing broken prompts in production.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t just speed—it’s that urgent fixes (like broken prompts already in prod) get stuck in a weekly queue while users suffer. A better alternative: run the scan *before* merge, but with a fast-path override for critical fixes, logged and reviewed retroactively. Settle it by testing both: measure how often urgent changes are blocked vs. how many broken prompts slip through.

name: Sprocket

Do this: Run the scan *before* merge, but let the lead push critical fixes straight to production with a logged override. This catches broken prompts early without blocking urgent work—speed matters when users are impacted. The trade-off is risk: we accept a small chance of a bad prompt slipping through, but we log and review overrides immediately to catch mistakes fast. Testing the bot on a small batch first proves the override works before we scale it.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t just a bad prompt slipping through—it’s that the override becomes a backdoor, eroding the discipline of pre-merge scanning. A better alternative: enforce pre-merge scanning for all changes, but add a *time-bound* emergency override (e.g., 1-hour max delay) with mandatory retroactive review. Settle it by measuring how often the override is used and the severity of incidents it prevents.
